emerging_technology: Satellite imaging spectroscopy for methane point-source detection
intended_application: Prioritize field inspections at three municipal landfills
capabilities_constraints: No field crew or geospatial analyst, contractor visits monthly; sites lack surveyed boundaries. No funding for extra callouts.
risk_consequence_context: Misattribution could send a contractor to the wrong facility; individual alerts may expire before its visit.
management_question: Should public alerts drive unscheduled contractor visits?
additional_context:
Fictional management scenario. Landscape as of 2026-11-16. Reference register checked on this date:
E1 Reuland et al., Nature | 2026-10-15 | independent single-blind experiment | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11115-0 | In 746 controlled events in Arizona, targeted instruments performed best at known locations. Cloud and instrument choice affected results. | Measured performance at the test site does not establish local observation frequency or detection of diffuse emissions.
E2 UNEP IMEO, Satellite Monitoring | 2026-05-04 expansion | programme operator | https://www.unep.org/en/what-we-do/energy/methane/methane-alert-and-response-system-mars | MARS expanded alerts to waste and coal in 2026, making a public alert route relevant to landfill operators. | Sector eligibility gives no promised service level for a particular site.
E3 NASA JPL, First Greenhouse Gas Plumes | 2024-10-10 | mission partner observation | https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/first-greenhouse-gas-plumes-detected-with-nasa-designed-instrument/ | Tanager-1 imaged a methane plume from a Karachi landfill on 19 September 2024. | One plume demonstrates feasibility. JPL designed the instrument and is a mission partner.
